sm: Dr. Jeffrey Long explains how he became interested in near-death experiences in 1984, after finding a medical journal article by a cardiologist describing patients who accurately reported events around them during cardiac arrest. He defines a near-death experience as a highly lucid, organized experience occurring when a person is unconscious or clinically dead. Drawing on more than four thousand cases he has collected since starting his organization and website in 1998, he lists common elements: an out-of-body experience, a tunnel, a mystical light, deceased loved ones, telepathic communication, a life review, and feelings of peace and love. He argues that what is real is what is seen consistently across many observations. He adds that, raised in a scientific household, he believes extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

Long says the serious study of near-death experiences took off after Raymond Moody's 1975 book Life After Life, and that hundreds of scholarly articles have since appeared. He notes that better resuscitation techniques and wider public acceptance mean more people survive and share their stories, and he cites a 2021 Pew survey in which 72 percent of American adults saw these experiences as an essence leaving the body. He then describes lines of evidence from his book on the afterlife: accurate out-of-body observations made far from the body, experiences during general anesthesia, and experiences reported when the heart has stopped and brain activity is flat. He also describes a woman named Vicki, blind from birth, who reported a highly visual experience with three hundred sixty degree vision.
